locator: Section 11.2.1 'Detecting and neutralizing a failed leader', p.150
claim: The dissertation states that in all practical settings a failed server cannot be distinguished from a slow server, which it calls the key characteristic of an asynchronous system.
quote: In all practical settings, it is impossible to distinguish a failed server from a slow server; this is the key characteristic of an asynchronous system.

locator: Section 11.2.1 'Detecting and neutralizing a failed leader', p.151
claim: A failure detector can wrongly report a leader as failed when it is merely slow, so the suspected leader must be neutralized.
quote: Since failure detectors can mistakenly report the leader as having failed when it is in fact slow, a suspected leader must be neutralized.

locator: Lecture 6 notes, 'Can we have the replicas elect a new primary'
claim: In the naive primary/backup scheme, if the backup decides the primary is down and takes over as coordinator while the primary is still running, a network partition produces split brain: two servers each acting as coordinator.
quote:
Can we have the replicas elect a new primary
  how about two servers, S1 and S2
  if both are up, S1 is in charge, forwards decisions to S2
  if S2 sees S1 is down, S2 takes over as coordinator
  what could go wrong?
  network partition! split brain!

locator: Section 11.2.1 'Detecting and neutralizing a failed leader', p.151
claim: A failover system must neutralize a suspected old leader: once a server has seen a larger term (or proposal/view/epoch) number, it will no longer accept requests from a leader with a smaller number.
quote: Once a server has seen a larger number, it will no longer accept requests from a leader with a smaller number.

locator: Section 6.4.1 'Using clocks to reduce messaging for read-only queries', p.74
claim: A lease-based fence assumes a bound on how far two machines' clocks can drift apart over a period, which is exactly what a timestamp-based check would have to trust.
quote: The lease approach assumes a bound on clock drift across servers (over a given time period, no server's clock increases more than this bound times any other).

locator: Section 2.1 'Achieving fault tolerance with replicated state machines', p.6, third properties bullet
claim: Raft does not depend on timing to keep the logs consistent; faulty clocks and extreme message delays can at worst cause availability problems, since safety holds under an asynchronous model where messages and processors proceed at arbitrary speeds.
quote: They do not depend on timing to ensure the consistency of the logs: faulty clocks and extreme message delays can, at worst, cause availability problems. That is, they maintain safety under an asynchronous model [71], in which messages and processors proceed at arbitrary speeds.

claim: Raft invalidates a stale leader with term numbers rather than clocks: a candidate or leader that learns its term is out of date immediately reverts to follower, and a server rejects any request carrying a stale term number.
quote: If a candidate or leader discovers that its term is out of date, it immediately reverts to follower state. If a server receives a request with a stale term number, it rejects the request.
